chapters.title: Chapter 3: The Term Structure of Volatility

lessons.title: IV Across Expiries: Building the Term Structure Curve

children.text: The Second Dimension: Same Strike, Different Expiry

Implied volatility is really a function of two inputs, strike and time to expiry, written IV(K, T). Chapter 2 held T fixed and varied K, which produced the skew. This chapter does the opposite: hold K fixed at the ATM strike and vary T instead. Read across every expiry Nifty actually trades, and ATM IV is no more constant than it was across strikes. That curve, ATM IV plotted against time to expiry, is called the term structure of volatility, and this lesson is about how you actually build one.
What Expiries Are Actually on the Table

On any given day, Nifty and Bank Nifty options trade across several live expiries at once: the nearest weekly expiry, the one after it, a monthly expiry, and sometimes a further-out quarterly expiry too. NSE's exact weekly expiry day has changed more than once over the years, so check the current NSE circular or your broker's contract specifications rather than assuming a fixed weekday. What has stayed consistent is where the volume actually sits: liquidity concentrates overwhelmingly in the nearest one or two weekly expiries, the same retail-driven weekly options boom from Chapter 2. Monthly and quarterly expiries trade too, but far more thinly, which matters the moment you try to trust an ATM IV reading from one of them.

body.text: A far-dated expiry's ATM IV is not automatically less reliable than a near-dated one, but it is more often thinly traded on the Indian market specifically, given how heavily volume concentrates in the nearest weeklies. The same checklist from Chapter 1, checking volume, OI, and bid-ask width before trusting a number, applies just as much across expiries as it does across strikes.

children.text: Building the Curve: One ATM IV Per Expiry

Mechanically, building a term structure is simple to describe, even if pulling clean live data takes some care. For every expiry you want on the curve, find its ATM strike (the strike nearest to the current spot price), read that expiry's ATM IV, the same expiry-tile figure from Chapter 1, Lesson 4, and plot it against how many days remain until that expiry. Repeat for every expiry you have decent liquidity in, and connect the points.

body.caption: Illustrative Nifty term structure snapshot (Spot: 24,800, same day, four live expiries)

children.text: This particular curve slopes upward, longer-dated ATM IV sitting above shorter-dated ATM IV, a shape borrowed from futures-curve language and called contango. A curve sloping the other way, short-dated IV higher than long-dated, is called backwardation. This lesson is only about recognizing that the curve exists and knowing how to build it; the next lesson goes into exactly why a curve leans one way or the other on any given day.
The Curve Is a Slice, Not the Whole Story

Notice what this curve quietly assumes: it only ever looks at the ATM strike. But Chapter 2 already showed that every one of these expiries has its own full skew, ATM is just one point on each expiry's own curve across strikes. Hold that thought. A term structure is really just the ATM slice of something bigger: every expiry has an entire skew, and stacking all of those skews together, across every expiry at once, is precisely the volatility surface this course builds toward in Chapter 4.

body.label: What this chapter's curve holds fixed, and what varies
body.value: Strike fixed at ATM; only time to expiry changes
body.context: Chapter 2's skew did the opposite: expiry fixed, strike varied. Put both dimensions together, strike and time, varying at once, and you get the full volatility surface covered in Chapter 4.

body.title: Skew or term structure?
body.question: Chapter 2 explained why Nifty's ATM IV differs from the IV of a strike 400 points out of the money, in the same expiry. This chapter's term structure instead compares ATM IV...
options: ...across different strikes within the same single expiry
...for roughly the same (ATM) moneyness across different expiries, holding strike distance fixed while time to expiry changes
...between Nifty and Bank Nifty on the same trading day
...between the call side and the put side at one specific strike
body.explanation: Skew (Chapter 2) fixes the expiry and varies the strike. Term structure (this chapter) fixes the strike, usually at ATM, and varies the expiry instead. They are two different one-dimensional slices through the same underlying IV(K, T) surface.

body.title: Two different numbers, same index, same day
body.scenario: A trader checks Nifty's option chain and finds an ATM IV of 10.85% for this week's expiry and 12.50% for the monthly expiry, a full 30 days out, on the exact same trading day. She is confused why "the same index" would show two different IV numbers at the same time.
body.prompt: Explain to her why this is completely normal, and name the shape this particular curve is showing.
body.modelAnswer: Each expiry trades as its own separate set of options, with its own supply, demand, and hedging flow, so there is no reason ATM IV has to match across expiries any more than it has to match across strikes within one expiry. Here, IV rises steadily as time to expiry increases, from 10.85% at 7 days out to 12.50% at 30 days out, which makes this a curve in contango, an upward-sloping term structure. The specific reasons a market leans into contango or backwardation on a given day are covered in the next lesson; for now, the key habit is simply expecting IV to be quoted per expiry, never as one fixed number for the underlying as a whole.

columns.label: Skew (Chapter 2)
points: Plotted as IV vs strike, delta, or moneyness, for one expiry
Driven mainly by asymmetric crash and tail-risk demand across strikes
Answers: how does IV differ by how far a strike sits from spot?

columns.label: Term Structure (this chapter)
points: Holds strike fixed, usually at ATM, varies expiry
Plotted as IV vs days (or years) to expiry
Driven mainly by how uncertainty is expected to evolve over time, the next lesson's subject
Answers: how does IV differ by when the option actually expires?

body.text: A single IV number can never describe an option chain honestly, not across strikes and not across expiries either. Skew is IV's answer to "how far." Term structure is its answer to "how long." A real trading desk reads both before it ever prices a single trade.

points: Term structure plots ATM IV against time to expiry, holding strike (moneyness) roughly fixed, the mirror image of skew, which holds expiry fixed and varies strike.
Building the curve means pulling the ATM IV for every actively traded expiry, near weekly, next weekly, monthly, and quarterly where available, and plotting it against days to expiry.

In India specifically, liquidity concentrates heavily in the nearest one or two weekly expiries; monthly and quarterly ATM IV readings can be thinner and less reliable, so the Chapter 1 liquidity checklist still applies.

An upward-sloping curve, longer-dated IV higher, is called contango; a downward-sloping curve is called backwardation, borrowing futures-curve terminology; the next lesson explains why each shape appears.

Term structure and skew are two different one-dimensional slices of the same underlying IV(K, T) object; stacking every expiry's full skew curve together is what actually builds the volatility surface in Chapter 4.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. The term structure table and chart are hypothetical and illustrative, continuing the running Nifty example from earlier chapters, and do not represent live NSE data. Expiry conventions and weekly expiry days can change; always confirm current contract specifications on NSE's website or your broker's terminal before trading, and consult a SEBI-registered advisor for personalised advice.
